Infectious Disease > General Infectious Disease Monoclonal for Dengue Shows Promise in Hospitalized Cases — Phase II results demonstrate preliminary evidence of benefit against mosquito-borne infection by Terrence Rudd, Staff Writer, MedPage Today August 25, 2026 • 3 min read Add MedPage Today on Google MedpageToday Key Takeaways There are licensed vaccines to prevent dengue but no approved antiviral to treat individuals who contract the mosquito-borne infection. In this mid-stage trial of adults hospitalized with dengue, a novel monoclonal antibody significantly reduced viral loads compared with placebo. Patients were also more likely to have their fever clear up in 24 hours with the monoclonal antibody. An investigational monoclonal antibody targeting dengue virus (Dengue-mAb) safely reduced viral loads and infection symptoms, according to a placebo-controlled phase II trial in India. Among 249 adults hospitalized with dengue and a history of fever, those randomized to one of four doses of Dengue-mAb achieved significantly greater viral log reductions 24 hours after treatment compared with placebo. The differences in adjusted least squares means were: 0.77 lower for 3 mg/kg (P=0.02) 1.12 lower for 5 mg/kg (P=0.003) 1.16 lower for 7 mg/kg (P<0.001) 1.21 lower for 9 mg/kg (P=0.001) Dengue-mAb, given as a single-dose intravenous infusion, also outperformed placebo when it came to reducing the presence of virus in the blood. Eight hours after treatment, 50% of placebo patients were negative for viremia compared with 71.4% for the 3 mg/kg group and 100% for the three higher-dose groups. No one in any of the study's five groups had a treatment-related serious adverse event, reported researchers led by Prasad Kulkarni, MD, of Serum Institute of India in Pune, in JAMA Network Open. "This is, to our knowledge, the first evidence of a preliminary therapeutic effect in patients with dengue," Kulkarni and colleagues wrote. "Although the number of patients is small, the observed significant reductions in viremia, RNAemia, and fever clearance may lead to reduction in severity of illness and decline in transmission of dengue." Transmitted through mosquito bites, dengue virus infection is the fastest-growing mosquito-borne disease globally. There were a record 14.1 million dengue cases and 9,508 deaths reported worldwide in 2024, with a 0.07% case fatality rate. Dengue is more common in tropical and subtropical regions, but reported U.S. dengue cases surged in 2024, climbing to 3,798 cases that year, up sharply from an annual average of 828 cases during 2010-2023, according to the CDC. Most infections are asymptomatic or mild, with common symptoms including headache, fever, body aches, nausea, and rash, but severe dengue can cause neurologic complications, such as Guillain-Barré syndrome, and death. There are three licensed vaccines to prevent dengue but no approved antiviral to treat it. Standard therapeutic approaches include pain management and hydration. The study enrolled 250 adult patients at 12 tertiary-care hospitals in India from September 2021 to May 2023 (one randomized participant withdrew consent before dosing and was excluded from the full analysis). Patients were ages 18 to 60 years, presented to a hospital within 48 hours after onset of fever, and had dengue confirmed through a rapid antigen test. The study's primary outcomes were viral log reductions at 24 hours after treatment, and the percentage of patients with causally related serious adverse events. Among the patients with fever at baseline, 92.9% of the 3 mg/kg group, 100% of both the 5 mg/kg and 7 mg/kg groups, and 94.1% of the 9 mg/kg group had fever clearance 24 hours after treatment, compared with 58.3% of the placebo recipients. In patients who had dengue virus RNA in the blood at baseline (roughly half of each group), 7.4% of placebo patients were negative 24 hours later, compared with 29.2% of patients randomized to Dengue-mAb 3 mg/kg, 28% of the 5 mg/kg group, 25% of the 7 mg/kg group, and 22.7% of the 9 mg/kg group. Overall, 23.3% of patients had an adverse event, including 20% of those in the placebo group and 20% to 32% of those in the four Dengue-mAb groups. All 13 treatment-related adverse events were in Dengue-mAb patients, but all recovered with no sequelae. Study limitations, according to Kulkarni and co-authors, included lower than predicted baseline viremia and RNAemia, which may indicate that participants were treated more than 48 hours after fever onset. Here’s What To Know About Dengue Keep an eye out for warning signs and seek medical advice if you're concerned. By Khirthnadhevi Kumar | 24 Aug 2026, 06:04 PM Share Share −Enlarge text+ #dengue #denguefever #health #lifestyle #panadol #sponsored #sponsored:panadol:240826 Cover image via National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases/Unsplash & Timur Weber/Pexels Follow us on Instagram, TikTok, and WhatsApp for the latest stories and breaking news. Malaysia is seeing a worrying increase in dengue cases Image via Vitaly Gariev/ Pexels Between 1 January and 9 July 2026, 42,848 dengue cases were reported across Malaysia. This marked a 34.8% increase from 31,790 cases during the same period last year. Even more concerning, dengue-related deaths rose from 19 to 34, marking a 78.9% increase. With Aedes mosquitoes thriving in Malaysia's hot and humid climate, dengue remains a public health concern. But how does dengue spread, what should you look out for, and what should you do if you suspect you have it? Here's what to know: 1. Dengue is a viral infection transmitted through the bite of an infected Aedes mosquito The virus does not normally spread directly from one person to another. Instead, a mosquito can pick up the virus after biting someone who has dengue, then transmit it to another person through a later bite. And getting dengue once does not mean you're protected for life. There are four dengue virus serotypes: DENV-1, DENV-2, DENV-3 and DENV-4. Being infected with one type does not protect you against the others, meaning a person can be infected multiple times. 2. Symptoms usually appear four to 10 days after a mosquito bite and may last between two and seven days Image via National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases Common symptoms include: High fever of around 40°C Severe headache Pain behind the eyes Muscle and joint pain Nausea or vomiting Rash ᅠ Since some of these symptoms can look like an ordinary viral infection, it's important not to simply brush them off, especially if the fever is high or several symptoms appear together. 3. The fever subsiding doesn't always mean you're recovering Severe dengue can develop when the fever starts to subside, so feeling better after the fever comes down does not necessarily mean the danger has passed. Seek immediate medical attention if you experience: Severe abdominal pain Persistent vomiting Bleeding from the nose or gums Blood in vomit or stool Restlessness Extreme fatigue or weakness ᅠ If these warning signs appear, don't wait for them to pass on their own. 4. There is no specific cure for dengue, so treatment focuses on managing symptoms and staying hydrated The World Health Organization and Malaysia's Ministry of Health recommend paracetamol to help relieve fever, headaches, muscle aches and joint pain. It can help with pain and fever without increasing the risk of bleeding. But not every common fever medicine is suitable. People with suspected or confirmed dengue should avoid aspirin, ibuprofen and other NSAIDs, as these may increase the risk of bleeding and other complications. In short: For dengue-related fever and pain, choose paracetamol and avoid NSAIDs such as aspirin and ibuprofen. If you've been diagnosed with dengue, giving your body enough time and care to recover is important Image via Engin Akyurt/Pexels Make sure to drink plenty of water, get enough rest, and use paracetamol appropriately to help manage fever and pain. However, keep an eye on how you're feeling. If your symptoms worsen or you notice any warning signs, seek medical attention promptly. You may not be able to keep every mosquito away, but a few simple habits can help reduce your risk of getting bitten To protect yourself from mosquito bites: Wear long-sleeved clothing Use mosquito repellent containing DEET, Picaridin, or IR3535 Use mosquito nets where appropriate ᅠ It's also important to make your home less inviting to Aedes mosquitoes, which can breed in containers holding stagnant water. Start by removing items that can collect water, disposing of solid waste properly, and covering, emptying and cleaning domestic water storage containers every week. With dengue cases and deaths on the rise, knowing the symptoms and warning signs could help you act sooner if you or someone around you becomes unwell If you develop a high fever along with dengue-like symptoms, don't brush it off. content: Dengue infections in Malaysia have surged 56.2 per cent this year, with 58,079 cases and 55 deaths recorded so far, even as take-up of the dengue vaccine remains low. Dr Shanmuganathan TV Ganeson, president of the Federation of Private Medical Practitioners’ Associations, Malaysia, said cost was one factor behind the low vaccine uptake. A two-dose regime could cost between 420 and 500 ringgit (US$104 to US$124), depending on the facility, and was generally cheaper in general practitioner clinics, he said, adding that GPs also lag larger facilities in terms of publicity. The dengue vaccine also had to compete with other vaccines that were more affordable, he said, especially the flu vaccine. “People here tend to opt for flu protection, especially travellers, which costs less than 100 ringgit, rather than an expensive dengue vaccine,” Shanmuganathan said. He explained that the dengue vaccine could not be given to pregnant women, breastfeeding mothers or immunocompromised patients and was recommended only for those aged between four and 60. View in App READ FULL ARTICLE Dengue Prevention Advocacy Malaysia co-chairman Professor Zamberi Sekawi said there was some hesitancy, as with other vaccines, but cautioned against reading the low uptake as anti-vaccine sentiment. A pest control worker sprays insecticide to help control the spread of dengue fever carried by mosquitoes in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, in 2014. Photo: Reuters “The evidence suggests that many Malaysians are undecided rather than opposed. They want to know how effective the vaccine is, its long-term safety, and the recommendation of their doctor,” he said, adding that public awareness of the vaccine was limited. “Cost and access must not be mistaken for hesitancy. Since we have to pay for it, it creates an additional barrier.” He said studies had shown that acceptance of the vaccine improved when people understood its risks and when doctors themselves recommended the jab. “We need better public education and, importantly, doctors who are confident enough to have personalised conversations about dengue prevention and vaccination,” he said. Checks by local reporters on prices at various private facilities found that two doses of the dengue vaccine can cost up to 480 ringgit. The Health Ministry said last year that it had no immediate plans to include the vaccine in the National Immunisation Programme. High-risk regions In a statement issued on Friday, the Health Ministry said the increase in cases was initially concentrated in the Klang Valley region, particularly Selangor state, as well as the federal territories of Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya. “The risk of dengue transmission remains high and the national situation remains worrying following increases in cases now also detected in several other states,” it said. Intensive, targeted prevention and control measures, including early case detection, vector control, outbreak management and personnel mobilisation, had since begun to show positive results, the ministry noted. The northern state of Perlis recorded the highest percentage increase, up 207 per cent from 55 cases between January and August last year to 169 this year. Johor’s cases more than doubled, climbing 109 per cent from 4,140 to 8,639, while Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya recorded a 106 per cent increase, from 5,013 to 10,316 cases. Selangor continued to be the worst-affected state in absolute terms, with 25,090, up 61 per cent from 15,610 cases. Sabah recorded 3,753 cases, up 34 per cent from 2,806 previously. Only Penang, Melaka and Kedah recorded reductions, with cases falling by 26 per cent, 36 per cent and 60 per cent, respectively. The ministry attributed the rise in dengue cases to several factors, including weather favourable to mosquito breeding. This article was first published by The Star

Reporter Tempo.co August 26, 2026 | 09:43 am Share Article link copied TEMPO.CO, Jakarta - Several posts claiming that the dengue fever vaccine contains artificial intelligence technology and tiny chips have circulated on Facebook via account 1 [archive] and account 2. These posts proliferated after Indonesia launched the world's first mRNA-based dengue vaccine prototype on July 8, 2026. The accounts claimed that the mRNA-based vaccine candidate contained nanobots, microchips, 5G or 6G devices, and Internet of Things technology. These components were alleged to alter human DNA. The posts urged the public to avoid hospitals and turn to herbal remedies instead. Is it true that the mRNA dengue vaccine candidate contains artificial intelligence (AI) and chips capable of altering human DNA? FACT CHECK Tempo’s fact checking team verified the claim through expert interviews and searches of credible sources. The findings indicate that the mRNA-based dengue vaccine candidate contains no microchips and does not alter human DNA. Artificial intelligence technology is utilized during the research process, not as an ingredient in the vaccine itself. The development of the mRNA-based dengue vaccine is a collaboration between the University of Indonesia and Tsinghua University. The lead researcher from the University of Indonesia, Prof. Dra. Beti Ernawati Dewi, stated that this tetravalent vaccine incorporates four antigen components derived from the four dengue virus serotypes found in Indonesia: DENV-1, DENV-2, DENV-3, and DENV-4. Beti explained that the research was designed because dengue fever remains a national health threat. "The vision is to build national self-reliance in facing dengue," Beti said in a written message to Tempo on Tuesday, August 18, 2026. Citing Antara, the Ministry of Health recorded 39,672 cases of dengue fever with 105 deaths up to May 2026. Throughout 2025, the number of cases reached 131,393, with 544 deaths. mRNA Vaccines Do Not Contain AI or Chips Beti Ernawati Dewi emphasized that artificial intelligence (AI) technology is used solely as a research tool to map viral mutations and design formulas. "Artificial intelligence is not an ingredient injected into the body," Beti stated. Researchers feed data into the AI system, including the virus's genetic structure, locations where it was found, and immune response characteristics. The AI system then analyzes patterns of viral changes to serve as a reference for updating antigens. Virologist Arif Nur Muhammad Ansori from Airlangga University added that mRNA vaccines do not contain nanobots, microchips, or electronic devices. The protective component for the mRNA utilizes lipid nanoparticles—which are purely fat particles—rather than electronic nanobot devices. mRNA Vaccines Do Not Alter Human DNA In general, according to the World Health Organization (WHO), vaccines contain ingredients such as antigens, preservatives, stabilizers, surfactants, diluents, and adjuvants. Antigens are components that trigger an immune response. In conventional vaccine technologies, antigens could be small parts of the disease-causing organism—such as proteins or sugars—or the entire organism in a weakened or inactivated form. In contrast, mRNA-based vaccines use genetic material (DNA or RNA) that instructs the body to produce specific antigens. According to Beti Ernawati Dewi, mRNA vaccines do not use live dengue viruses capable of causing infection. Conceptually, the mRNA carries temporary genetic information that enables cells to produce dengue antigens, thereby stimulating the immune system. Beti explained that mRNA is not designed to alter human DNA. Once injected into the body, mRNA operates outside the cell nucleus to provide instructions for producing antigens—substances that trigger the human immune system. After performing its function, the mRNA molecule naturally degrades. "mRNA vaccines are not designed to remain permanently in the body," she said. Conclusion The claim that mRNA vaccines are combined with AI, nanobots, microchips, 5G/6G, and IoT is false. **Do you have information or claims that you want to have fact-checked? content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Wednesday, August 26, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health IDAMS Study Improves Early Prediction of Severe Dengue Outcomes by Bioengineer August 21, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 5 mins read 0 Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Dengue fever is entering a new era of clinical risk assessment as researchers seek to identify, as early as possible, which patients are likely to deteriorate. A study by L. Phung Khanh, K.D. Rosenberger, T. Dong Thi Hoai and colleagues, published in Nature Communications in 2026, examines how data from the prospective, multicentre IDAMS study can improve the prediction of adverse dengue outcomes. The work addresses one of the most persistent challenges in dengue medicine: most infections resolve without major complications, but a small and difficult-to-recognise proportion can progress rapidly to shock, severe bleeding, organ dysfunction or death. Dengue is caused by four closely related viruses known as dengue virus serotypes 1 through 4, all transmitted primarily by Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus mosquitoes. Infection commonly begins with fever, headache, muscle and joint pain, nausea and rash. The period when the fever subsides is particularly dangerous, however, because vascular leakage may intensify even as the patient appears to be improving. Fluid can move from the bloodstream into surrounding tissues, reducing circulating blood volume and placing the heart, kidneys and other organs under severe stress. In this narrow clinical window, timely recognition of risk is essential, yet early symptoms often overlap with those of uncomplicated dengue. Discover more infectious disease Health health risk The IDAMS, or International Research Consortium on Dengue Risk Assessment, prospective multicentre study was designed to collect clinical information from patients in different settings and follow them over time. Prospective studies are especially valuable for prediction research because information is recorded before the final outcome is known. This allows investigators to test whether early observations—rather than hindsight—can distinguish patients who will remain stable from those who will develop complications. A multicentre design also helps address a major limitation of many clinical prediction tools: a model developed in one hospital or country may perform less reliably when applied to populations with different ages, viral serotypes, coexisting illnesses, healthcare access and patterns of presentation. The new analysis focuses on improving early prediction for adverse outcomes, a task that requires more than simply identifying patients who are already critically ill. A clinically useful model must operate before severe deterioration becomes obvious, using information available during the first assessment or early follow-up. Potentially informative variables in dengue research include age, duration of fever, warning symptoms, blood pressure, pulse pressure, capillary refill, fluid intake and output, bleeding signs and laboratory measurements such as platelet count, haematocrit and white blood cell levels. The scientific challenge is to determine which combinations carry genuine predictive value, how their importance changes over the course of illness and how to avoid confusing common dengue features with specific signals of danger. Platelet counts illustrate the difficulty. A falling platelet level is widely associated with dengue progression, but thrombocytopenia alone does not reliably identify patients who will develop shock or organ failure. Haematocrit can provide information about haemoconcentration and plasma leakage, yet its interpretation depends on a patient’s baseline level, hydration status and any bleeding that may be occurring. Similarly, fever duration and the appearance of abdominal pain or persistent vomiting may be informative, but their predictive meaning can vary between patients. Robust risk models must therefore integrate multiple clinical and laboratory signals instead of relying on a single laboratory threshold. The study’s importance lies in its effort to refine that integrated approach using data gathered across multiple centres. Prediction models can be expressed in several ways, including statistical risk scores, regression-based algorithms or more complex machine-learning systems. Regardless of the method, performance must be assessed carefully. Researchers typically examine discrimination—how well a model separates higher-risk from lower-risk patients—and calibration, which measures whether predicted probabilities correspond to outcomes observed in practice. A model that ranks patients correctly but consistently overestimates risk may lead to unnecessary admissions, while one that underestimates danger could delay monitoring and treatment. For dengue, such distinctions have immediate implications for health systems. During seasonal epidemics, hospitals may receive more patients than they can safely observe. Over-triage can consume beds, staff time and laboratory capacity, while under-triage can leave vulnerable patients without sufficient monitoring during the critical phase of illness. An improved early-warning system could help clinicians decide who requires frequent reassessment, intravenous-fluid monitoring, laboratory follow-up or transfer to a higher level of care. It could also support safer outpatient management for patients whose early profiles indicate a lower probability of severe complications, provided that they receive clear instructions and rapid access to care if symptoms change. The use of data from a prospective multicentre cohort is also relevant to the broader movement toward transportable and equitable clinical prediction. A model must be tested not only on the population from which it was derived but also across different demographic and epidemiological contexts. Dengue severity can be influenced by previous infection with another serotype, immune status, age and underlying conditions, including pregnancy and chronic cardiovascular, renal or metabolic disease. Geographic variation may affect the timing of presentation and the prevalence of circulating serotypes. By drawing on multicentre evidence, the IDAMS analysis seeks to make early prediction more representative of the patients encountered in real-world dengue care rather than narrowly optimised for a single institution. The findings are expected to contribute to a more precise understanding of how early clinical data can be converted into actionable risk information. Their value will ultimately depend on external validation, ease of use and integration into routine care. A prediction tool that requires tests unavailable in rural clinics, or that produces a probability without clear guidance for clinicians, may have limited practical impact. Conversely, a transparent model based on readily obtainable observations could be incorporated into triage protocols, electronic medical records and outbreak-response systems. As dengue expands into new regions under the influence of urbanisation, travel and changing climate conditions, reliable early assessment may become as important as antiviral development in reducing preventable complications. The IDAMS study therefore represents a step toward treating dengue not as a single uniform illness but as a dynamic infection whose risks change from day to day. By improving the ability to recognise patients on a dangerous trajectory before severe disease is fully established, the research could strengthen clinical surveillance and help direct limited resources to those most likely to need them. The work also highlights a central principle of viral medicine: better outcomes often depend not only on discovering new therapies, but on extracting more precise information from the earliest stages of infection. And the rate of women among members is 38 percent. Women's answer review because IDCR and the Department of Health. Muhammad Shafiullah Published: 3:37 PM, 24 August 2026 Bangladesh dengue deaths: Women account for 59% of fatalities Muhammad Shafiullah Published : 24 August 2026, 15:37 File Photo Women have accounted for 59% of dengue deaths in Bangladesh this year, despite representing only 38% of total infections, prompting the Institute of Epidemiology, Disease Control and Research (IEDCR) and the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) to begin reviewing the causes of female deaths. DGHS data for this year show that dengue infections and deaths have been rising since July. While more men have been infected, more women have died. Women of reproductive and working age, particularly those aged 20 to 50, have recorded the highest number of deaths. A large share of total dengue deaths among women has occurred in the 21 to 50 age group. Analysis of updated DGHS dengue data from the start of the year to yesterday, Sunday, shows that 28,929 people were hospitalised with dengue across the country. Of them, 17,908 were men, or 62%, and 11,015 were women, or 38%. The mortality pattern was the reverse. A total of 82 people have died of dengue this year. Of them, 48 were women, accounting for more than 59% of all deaths, while men accounted for 41%. Statistics show that in city corporation areas, 26 of the 37 patients who died while under treatment were women, while 10 were men. Outside city corporation areas, 44 people died in hospitals, including 22 men and 22 women. The higher female death toll in urban areas is being attributed to possible delays or neglect in hospital admission and access to emergency treatment for women with dengue, compared with rural or small-town areas. Health sector experts say delayed hospital admission, failure to detect physical complications in time and neglect after infection from mosquito bites in domestic settings may be increasing women’s risk of death. In many cases, women do not go to hospital until symptoms become severe. Treatment becomes more complicated if patients are brought in only after platelet counts have fallen dangerously low or dengue shock syndrome has developed. Senior public health expert Professor Dr Abu Jamil Faisal told Ajker Patrika that no scientific conclusion has yet been reached on why women are dying in greater numbers. “An autopsy must be conducted. There is no alternative. Where autopsy is not possible, verbal autopsy should be done. That means speaking to the patient’s relatives to understand the final condition and reviewing treatment documents,” he said. Professor Faisal said women lag behind in access to healthcare and face neglect at every stage from the onset of illness. He said women often do not receive the treatment they should, due both to family neglect and their own lack of awareness and inattention. Referring to a similar pattern in 2023, he said the government still does not have data on why women died in higher numbers, calling it a failure and negligence by state institutions. He also said government agencies had failed to take effective steps to build awareness. IEDCR has intensified field investigations and laboratory-based research to determine whether the higher female mortality rate is linked to viral type, treatment delays or other causes, even though more men have been infected this year. Professor Dr Ahmed Nowsher Alam, Chief Scientific Officer (Virology) at IEDCR, said: “From the laboratory, we mainly work on dengue serotypes and positivity rates. This year, sample tests in Dhaka found the ‘DEN-3’ serotype more frequently. On the other hand, samples collected from Bandarban outside Dhaka showed more ‘DEN-2’.” He said sample collection, once largely centred on Dhaka, has now expanded to different parts of the country. On reviewing the causes of death, or conducting a “death review”, IEDCR Director Dr Kazi Ahmed Jaki said: “To clarify the actual causes of women’s deaths, we need to conduct a detailed death review. Last week, we received instructions to carry out a death review of those who died of dengue this year, and we have started planning with a team to analyse the causes and patterns of those deaths.” Dr Jaki said teams would visit hospitals to collect treatment records, speak to relatives and review medical information. The review will examine where gaps or delays occurred in treatment, when patients arrived at hospital and whether there was any deviation from prescribed treatment protocols, in order to identify the root causes. Professor Faisal, however, said autopsies would also be needed alongside the IEDCR review to determine the actual causes of women’s deaths. Dr Ashrafun Nahar, Deputy Director (Disease Control) and the designated DGHS official to speak to the media on dengue, said it would not be possible to say why more women were dying without a death review. She said every government hospital in the country has a death review committee, which examines when, how and in what condition a patient arrived at hospital and in what condition the patient died. She added that IEDCR is also working on the issue and that no conclusions can be drawn without reviewing what complications led to the deaths of women. Separate IEDCR findings show that the DENV-3 serotype has again become dominant in Bangladesh after several years. For the previous four years, DENV-2 had been the main dengue serotype. Analysis of 71 samples from hospitalised patients this year found DENV-3 in 91.5% of cases and DENV-2 in 8.5%. According to the World Health Organization, dengue virus has four serotypes: DENV-1, DENV-2, DENV-3 and DENV-4. Infection with one serotype creates lasting immunity only against that specific type. As a result, people who had previously developed antibodies to DENV-2 may be infected again with DENV-3. Public health experts have warned that a second infection with a different serotype may increase the risk of complications and dengue shock syndrome. They urged people not to ignore fever or symptoms and to seek testing and treatment quickly. One news app. Start reading Medical Daily Health Joseph James Aug 25, 2026, 1:00 AM Sixteen Local Dengue Cases Reported in a Single Week as Three Florida Counties Sit Under Alert Florida Hillsborough Hillsborough County EPA MiamiDade Pinellas A Case Count That More Than Tripled in Seven Days Florida reported 16 locally acquired dengue cases in a single week, a jump that brings the state's 2026 total to 23 and concentrates almost all of them in one county. The figures come from the Florida Arbovirus Surveillance report for Week 32 , covering August 9 through 15. Locally acquired means the person did not travel. The infection occurred in Florida, transmitted by a Florida mosquito. That is a different category of risk from the travel-associated cases that make up the overwhelming majority of dengue cases in the United States, and it is why state officials track these counts separately. The weekly jump reflects case reporting catching up rather than 16 people falling ill within seven days. Onset dates for the 23 local cases fall in July for 14 of them and in August for nine. Both readings matter. The reporting surge means the public picture available a week earlier understated what was already underway, and the August onsets mean transmission is current rather than historical. Three counties are now under a mosquito-borne illness alert: Hillsborough, Miami-Dade, and Pinellas. Four more, Alachua, Leon, Palm Beach, and Pasco, are under the lower-level advisory. Hillsborough Now Accounts for Most Local Transmission The county distribution is the part that deserves attention. Of the 23 locally acquired cases, Hillsborough County has 15. Miami-Dade has four, Pinellas has three, and Palm Beach has one. That puts about two-thirds of the state's local transmission this year in a single Tampa Bay county rather than in South Florida. The serotype data points to a single transmission chain rather than scattered introductions. Twenty-two of the 23 cases have been serotyped, 20 of them as DENV-2, and all 15 Hillsborough cases are DENV-2. When one serotype accounts for an entire county cluster, investigators are generally looking at sustained local circulation rather than repeated separate importations from returning travelers. Florida also logged 86 travel-associated dengue cases in 2026, with Cuba as the country of exposure for 55 of them. That imported burden is the reservoir from which local transmission begins. A traveler returns infected, a local mosquito bites during the window when the virus is in their blood, and that mosquito then bites someone else. CDC outlined this national risk pattern and updated testing advice in a 2025 health update on dengue in the United States . For residents of Tampa, St. Petersburg, Clearwater, and the surrounding communities, the practical shift is that dengue is no longer only a travel question at a doctor's visit. It is now a reasonable diagnosis to consider in someone with a fever who has not left the region. Infected Mosquitoes Found in the Neighborhood The surveillance finding that separates this from an ordinary case count is entomological. Five mosquito pools in Hillsborough County tested positive for dengue virus, collected on August 6 and August 11, all in Aedes aegypti and all DENV-2, matching the human cases. Finding a virus in trapped mosquitoes is stronger evidence than patient reports alone. It confirms that infected vectors are physically present in the environment rather than inferring transmission backward from illnesses. It also gives mosquito control districts a map for targeted treatment rather than blanket spraying. Aedes aegypti is a container breeder. It does not need ponds or marshland. It lays eggs in water held in a bottle cap, a plant saucer, a clogged gutter, a fold in a tarp, a birdbath, a discarded tire. It bites during daylight hours and stays close to homes rather than ranging widely. That behavior is why yard-level action matters more for this species than it does for the mosquitoes that carry West Nile virus. Risk is not evenly distributed. It concentrates in neighborhoods with dense housing, standing water on properties awaiting repair, and homes without intact window screens or air conditioning. People who work outdoors during daylight, including construction, landscaping, and delivery workers, face greater exposure than office workers. Bite Prevention and Symptom Thresholds State and federal health officials emphasize the same two-part approach in their guidance on preventing dengue : drain standing water around the home weekly and prevent bites using EPA-registered repellent, loose long-sleeved clothing, and intact screens and air conditioning. Tipping and tossing containers matter because breeding sites are small and easy to overlook. Many dengue infections cause no symptoms at all. Among people who do become ill, symptoms typically begin with sudden fever accompanied by severe headache, pain behind the eyes, muscle and joint pain, nausea, vomiting, or a rash, lasting two to seven days, with recovery in about a week. The threshold that matters most is the second phase. About one in 20 people who get sick with dengue develop severe dengue, a medical emergency that can develop within hours and often appears as the fever is coming down rather than at its peak. Warning signs that indicate severe dengue include severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, bleeding from the gums or nose, blood in vomit or stool, extreme fatigue or restlessness, and difficulty breathing. Anyone with those signs needs emergency care immediately. There is no specific antiviral treatment for dengue. Care is supportive, centered on fluids and monitoring. Aspirin and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs such as ibuprofen are generally avoided in suspected dengue because of the bleeding risk, and that is a decision to confirm with a clinician rather than make alone. National context helps calibrate. A federal surveillance report on United States dengue cases found that 97.2 percent of the 3,798 cases reported in 2024 from states and the District of Columbia were travel-associated, with locally acquired infections accounting for the remaining 2.8 percent. Florida issues its arbovirus surveillance report weekly, and the next edition will indicate whether the Hillsborough cluster is still growing. Key Questions Answered What is new? Florida reported 16 locally acquired dengue cases during the week of August 9 to 15, bringing the 2026 state total to 23 across four counties. Where are the cases? Hillsborough County has 15, Miami-Dade 4, Pinellas 3, and Palm Beach 1. Hillsborough, Miami-Dade, and Pinellas are under a mosquito-borne illness alert. Does "locally acquired" mean something different from "travel-related"? Yes. These patients did not travel. They were infected by mosquitoes in Florida, meaning the virus is circulating locally rather than only arriving with returning travelers. Has the virus been found in mosquitoes? Yes. Five Aedes aegypti mosquito pools in Hillsborough County tested positive for DENV-2, the same serotype found in all 15 Hillsborough patients. What symptoms should residents watch for? Sudden fever with severe headache, pain behind the eyes, muscle and joint pain, nausea, vomiting, or rash. Most people recover in about a week. When does dengue become an emergency? About one in 20 people who get sick develop severe dengue. Severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, bleeding, extreme fatigue or difficulty breathing require emergency care, and these signs often appear as the fever subsides. What can households do right now? Empty standing water weekly from containers as small as a bottle cap, use EPA-registered repellent, repair window screens, and cover skin during daylight hours when Aedes aegypti is most active. content: Thursday, August 27, 2026|82°F Partly Cloudy Breaking News IN THE DARK?: Aide says only Duterte, Lachica knew how confidential fund was used Aug 27 82°F Search Discover more Digital News Access Investigative Journalism Workshops Iloilo City Guide NEWS OPINION BUSINESS SPORTS FEATURES INITIATIVE POLICIES OTHERS ABOUT USCONTACT US Menu Daily Guardian News Opinion Business Sports Features Initiative Policies Others Home>news Single Dengvaxia dose cut severe dengue by 31% in Cebu 5 min readShare full article 0 By Francis Allan L. Angelo August 26, 2026 Updated August 25, 2026 By Francis Allan L. Angelo Children in Cebu who received only one dose of the dengue vaccine CYD-TDV before the Philippine government halted its mass immunization drive in 2017 were 31% less likely to develop more severe forms of dengue over the next five years, a University of the Philippines-led study found. The protection, as reported in the journal Vaccine, held from the 2017 vaccination through February 2023 and covered both dengue with warning signs and severe dengue, with a 95 percent confidence interval of 6 to 49 percent and a p-value of less than 0.0001. Against hospitalized virologically confirmed dengue overall, however, the single dose showed 21 percent effectiveness that did not reach statistical significance, with a confidence interval running from minus 7 percent to 41 percent and a p-value of 0.1129. The study also found that whatever protection the dose conferred was concentrated early. Effectiveness against hospitalized confirmed dengue was 49 percent in the first year after the mass vaccination, from February 15, 2018 to February 14, 2019, with a confidence interval of 19 to 68 percent and a p-value of 0.0067. It appeared to decline after that first year. Dengvaxia, the first dengue vaccine licensed for use, was introduced in the Philippines in 2016 for children aged nine to 14 years. The Department of Health was still rolling it out in Cebu province in 2017 when concerns about the vaccine’s safety in seronegative individuals prompted an abrupt halt, leaving many Cebu children with only the first of three scheduled doses. PhilippineNews Portal Researchers ran a matched case-control study in Cebu province from February 15, 2018 to February 28, 2023. Cases were children born between 2003 and 2008, resident in Cebu since the 2017 mass vaccination, eligible for the vaccine, and admitted to one of four participating government hospitals with fever of less than five days. Dengue was confirmed by real-time reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction, and illness was classified according to World Health Organization 2009 criteria as dengue, dengue with warning signs, or severe dengue. Two neighborhood controls of the same sex and age group were recruited for each case. Of 71,223 acute febrile presentations screened at the study hospitals, 69,978, or 98.3 percent, were ineligible. Of the 1,245 eligible episodes, 333, or 26.7 percent, were excluded because of consent refusal, withdrawal, or refusal of blood collection within five days of fever onset. The team enrolled 912 suspected dengue episodes, of which 620 tested positive by RT-PCR. Another 36 confirmed cases were dropped because matching controls could not be recruited, 13 of them because of mobility restrictions during the COVID-19 enhanced community quarantine. The final analysis covered 584 cases and 1,168 matched controls. Among the 584 confirmed cases, 397, or 67.8 percent, presented as dengue with warning signs, eight, or 1.4 percent, had severe dengue, and one child, or 0.2 percent, died. Beyond fever, the most common presumptive signs and symptoms were nausea or vomiting in 414 cases, or 70.9 percent, malaise in 373 cases, or 63.9 percent, and anorexia in 235 cases, or 40.2 percent. The most frequent warning sign was abdominal pain in 272 cases, or 46.6 percent, followed by lethargy in 158 cases, or 27.1 percent, and restlessness in 116 cases, or 19.9 percent. All four dengue serotypes circulated among the cases. Serotype 3 was the most common at 287 cases, or 49.1 percent, followed by serotype 2 at 166, serotype 1 at 86, and serotype 4 at 37. The researchers said no conclusions could be drawn about effectiveness by serotype because of inadequate sample size. Vaccination coverage differed between the two groups. Of the cases, 112, or 19.2 percent, had received a dose, compared with 270, or 23.1 percent, of the controls. The crude odds ratio was 0.74, and the adjusted odds ratio was 0.79 after controlling for dengue in the household, dengue in the neighborhood, concrete housing material, window screens, stagnant water, insect repellent use, and ownership of a bicycle and a computer. The five-year figures are lower than the interim results the same team reported through February 2020, which showed 26 percent effectiveness against hospitalized confirmed dengue and 51 percent against dengue with warning signs. The authors attributed the drop to waning vaccine protection. Both sets of estimates fall well below the 80 percent efficacy against hospitalized confirmed dengue recorded for the full three-dose regimen in this age group over two years. They are close, however, to the 26 percent single-dose effectiveness measured among people aged 19 to 27 within three years of a mass vaccination in Brazil. The study could not determine whether participants had been infected with dengue before vaccination, which the authors identified as an important limitation because Phase 3 trials found three-dose efficacy of 76 percent among seropositive children aged nine to 16 and 39 percent among seronegative children. The researchers said a large majority of the Cebu cohort was likely seropositive. The authors also flagged the COVID-19 pandemic as a source of bias, noting that lockdowns in 2020 and 2021 limited enrollment as hospitals prioritized COVID-19 cases and parents avoided bringing children in for care. Public reaction to the Dengvaxia controversy, including criminal investigations against those involved in the campaign, likely introduced further selection bias toward the null, the authors wrote, because some vaccinated patients were urged to seek treatment for milder illness that would otherwise have gone unhospitalized. The researchers concluded that the waning protection they measured underscores the need for the complete three-dose schedule to achieve sustained efficacy, and said policymakers should weigh the results when designing vaccination strategies in settings where baseline serostatus cannot be readily determined. The study sponsor, the University of the Philippines Manila, received funding from Sanofi, the vaccine’s manufacturer, to undertake the effectiveness assessment. Sanofi took part in discussions of the study design and reviewed the initial manuscript draft, but the authors said they retained complete autonomy over data analysis, interpretation, and submission. PhilippineNews Portal The study was led by Kristal An Agrupis and Maria Vinna Crisostomo as co-first authors, with Jedas Veronica Daag, March Helena Jane Lopez, Kiarah Louise Florendo, Clarissa de Guzman, Jacqueline Deen, and Michelle Ylade of the Institute of Child Health and Human Development, University of the Philippines–National Institutes of Health, Manila. Also on the team were Jesus Sarol Jr. of the Interdisciplinary Health Sciences Institute at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, Ava Kristy Sy of the Department of Virology at the Research Institute for Tropical Medicine in Muntinlupa, Zoraida Yurango of Cebu Provincial Hospital–Bogo, Olivia Dandan of Cebu Provincial Hospital–Balamban, and Jean Balabat of Eversley Childs Sanitarium and General Hospital in Mandaue City. infections and dengue complications. With hospitals reporting waitlists for beds, medical experts said the current season was proving more severe than the previous year.Dr Sagar Lad, a neonatologist and paediatric intensivist at Jehangir and Sahyadri Hospitals, said, “Most children in the ICU are suffering from complications related to dengue and influenza, specifically the H3N2 strain. Both ICUs and general wards are full, and we currently have patients on the waitlist,” he said.Dr Lad attributed the spike to the prevailing rainy and cloudy weather, which facilitates viral transmission. “While weather doesn’t increase the viral load itself, high humidity, limited sunlight, and people spending more time in close proximity indoors create the perfect environment for respiratory viruses to spread,” he said.The pressure is equally high in adult wards, where H1N1 (swine flu) has emerged as the leading cause of severe respiratory distress. by Taboolaby Taboola Sponsored LinksSponsored Links Promoted LinksPromoted Links You May Like Let ADT set up security while you settle inADT Shop Now Undo Dr Ameet Dravid, an infectious diseases specialist at Noble and Poona Hospitals, reported a marked increase in lower respiratory tract infections.“The majority of severe cases requiring ICU care are linked to H1N1, the pandemic strain. While most patients in outpatient departments present with typical upper respiratory symptoms like cough and cold, a significant portion is progressing to breathlessness and pneumonia,” Dr Dravid said. He added that while some Covid-19 and dengue patients are in the ICU, H1N1 remains the dominant threat.Data from the Pune Municipal Corporation’s (PMC) Metropolitan Surveillance Unit confirms a marked rise in H1N1 infections. While cases were negligible in the first quarter of 2026, they exploded in the monsoon months. Altogether, 225 cases have been recorded in August so far, compared with 35 in July, taking the 2026 total to 290 cases.Officials cautioned that the August figure is preliminary and likely to rise as data is updated. Doctors said these figures are a “vast underestimate,” as many patients with flu-like symptoms are treated without being officially tested for H1N1 or COVID-19.The surge has forced smaller nursing homes to take the overflow as major hospitals turn patients away. Dr Vijay Natarajan, medical superintendent at Deenanath Mangeshkar Hospital, said the facility has been operating beyond capacity for over a month.“This is an annual cycle where respiratory and mosquito-borne diseases peak between June and Oct. However, with a growing population and no proportionate increase in healthcare beds, the shortage is felt much more acutely now,” Dr Natarajan said.The severity of the current wave has drawn comparisons to previous outbreaks. Dr Kapil Zirpe, pulmonologist and head of the neurotrauma unit at Ruby Hall Clinic, said, “This year, the surge feels like 2009 and 2011. We are seeing patients on ventilators and oxygen support in very serious condition.”Dr Zirpe said the younger populations are particularly at risk of spreading the virus due to increased socialisation and a lack of precautions, such as masking. “Many dismiss it as a common cold until it becomes severe,” he warned.Doctors said complications typically arise as the infection progresses. While a baseline percentage of the population inevitably develops severe symptoms, the risk multiplies as the overall infection rate in the city grows. Immunocompromised individuals and the elderly remain the most vulnerable to severe outcomes due to underlying comorbidities.Dr Deepali Ambike, head of paediatrics at YCM Hospital, said their paediatric ICU is also full. “Children who deteriorate are developing pneumonia and requiring ventilatory support. content: Select Hans India Now Select Hans India Now Telangana+ Hyderabad Warangal Khamman Adilabad Manchiryal-Asifabad Nizamabad Karimnagar Medak-Sangareddy Siddipet Mahaboobnagar Nalgonda-Suryapet Andhra Pradesh+ Amaravati Visakhapatnam Tirupati Kurnool Guntur Anantapur Chittoor Eluru Kadapa Kakinada Nellore Ongole Rajahmundry Srikakulam National+ Karnataka Tamil Nadu Uttar Pradesh New Delhi Bengaluru Chennai Mumbai Kolkata Odisha Global Opinion+ Editorial Business+ Market Technology+ AI News Auto Entertainment+ OTT Tollywood Bollywood Lifestyle+ Health Womenia Spiritual Sports Videos+ Web Stories Edu and Careers+ Young Hans Hans Premium Telangana Hyderabad Warangal Khamman Adilabad Manchiryal-Asifabad Nizamabad Karimnagar Medak-Sangareddy Siddipet Mahaboobnagar Nalgonda-Suryapet Andhra Pradesh Amaravati Visakhapatnam Tirupati Kurnool Guntur Anantapur Chittoor Eluru Kadapa Kakinada Nellore Ongole Rajahmundry Srikakulam National Karnataka Tamil Nadu Uttar Pradesh New Delhi Bengaluru Chennai Mumbai Kolkata Odisha Global Opinion Editorial Business Market Technology AI News Auto Entertainment OTT Tollywood Bollywood Lifestyle Health Womenia Spiritual Sports Videos Web Stories Edu and Careers Young Hans Hans Premium Home Life Style Health Life Style Deccan Hospital sounds dengue alert; asks public to stay vigilant In Short Chief Consultant Physician Vamsee Krishna P outlines critical warning signs, preventive measures, and treatment protocols amid seasonal cases surge The Hans India Created On: 26 Aug 2026 4:35 AM ISTComment Share : X Deccan Hospital sounds dengue alert; asks public to stay vigilant A− Font size A+ Select Hans India Now FOLLOW ON Google News Hyderabad: Amid a sharp seasonal surge in dengue fever cases across urban neighbourhoods, Vamsee Krishna P, Chief Consultant Physician and Diabetologist at The Deccan Hospital Somajiguda, has urged the public to stay vigilant and informed. With over 15 years of clinical experience, Vamsee Krishna P emphasised early detection, proper medical care, and avoiding self-medication to combat the mosquito-borne illness. Dengue is a viral infection caused by a flavivirus with four distinct serotypes DENV-1, DENV-2, DENV-3, and DENV-4, primarily transmitted by day-biting Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus mosquitoes. Secondary infection with a different serotype significantly increases the risk of severe dengue. Initial signs appear 4 to 10 days after a mosquito bite, including sudden high fever up to 104 deg F, severe headache, pain behind the eyes, intense muscle and joint pain, and skin rash. The critical phase occurs around days 3 to 7 as fever subsides, during which blood vessels may leak fluid, causing dangerous blood pressure drops. Warning signs requiring emergency care include severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, bleeding gums or nose, blood in vomit or stool, and extreme fatigue, which often surface just as the initial fever drops. Treatment relies strictly on supportive care through rest and hydration, as no specific antiviral or antibiotic medication exists. Fever and pain must be managed using paracetamol, while aspirin and ibuprofen must be strictly avoided due to increased bleeding risks. Prevention involves clearing stagnant water weekly from pots, buckets, and coolers, wearing long-sleeved clothing, applying safe insect repellents, and using window screens or bed nets. Vaccines like Qdenga, available in endemic regions, will soon be available in India. Regarding platelet transfusions, Vamsee Krishna P clarified that transfusions are reserved strictly for patients with active bleeding or critically low counts under 10000 to 20000 per microlitre. Routine prophylactic transfusions for stable patients are avoided because transfused platelets degrade quickly in active dengue, carrying risks like fluid overload, allergic reactions, and lung injury, while most patients recover counts naturally. Hospitalisation is essential if patients experience severe stomach tenderness, persistent vomiting, mucosal bleeding, black tarry stool, extreme weakness, cold clammy skin, breathing difficulty, fever lasting past five days, rapid platelet drops, or when living far from medical monitoring. Highlighting that one bite brings multiple health risks, Vamsee Krishna P advised immediate consultation upon noticing symptoms to ensure a safe monsoon. content: Citrus County confirms first case of locally acquired Dengue fever Updated Sat, August 22, 2026 at 10:19 PM UTC CITRUS COUNTY, Fla. (WFLA) — The Florida Department of Health in Citrus County announced Saturday its first confirmed case of Dengue fever. According to the DOH, Dengue can present as a flu-like illness with severe muscle aches and joint pain, fever, and sometimes a rash. There are usually no respiratory symptoms. Health officials said Dengue fever is not contagious but is transmitted through the bite of an infected Aedes aegypti mosquito. Symptoms appear within 15 days after being bitten. Eight cases were confirmed in Hillsborough County , with two additional cases reported in Pinellas County. DOH is coordinating surveillance and prevention efforts with Citrus County Mosquito Control through treatments such as increased truck fogging, aerial larviciding and localized ground inspections for breeding locations. Health officials encouraged the community to avoid mosquito bites by taking basic precautions such as wearing protective clothing and applying insect repellents registered by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency. DOH also said to repair damaged screening on windows, doors, porches, and patios. Drain water from garbage cans, buckets, or any other containers where sprinkler or rainwater has collected. content: Some Kern County scientists and mosquito-abatement professionals are acknowledging that dengue fever, a mosquito-borne illness also known as "breakbone fever," will likely be seen in locally acquired cases in Kern County. Mark Dery, scientific program director at Kern Mosquito Abatement & Vector Control District, told The Californian in an email that Aedes aegypti, the newest local mosquito discovered in Kern a dozen years ago, is "firmly established in Kern County," meaning the potential exists for travel cases to result in local transmission. Travel-associated cases are contracted in another country or region where dengue is common, then brought home by the traveler, while local transmission cases (locally acquired) are caught from infected mosquitoes within the local area. "With dengue infections being relatively common in many parts of the world, it is likely that California will continue to have periodic outbreaks of local dengue transmission," Dery said, referring to locally acquired cases that first began in Southern California in 2023. Despite the arrival of dengue in the Golden State, overall risk of infection remains low and it is unlikely that dengue will become established in California, Dery said. According to records compiled by the California Department of Public Health, Kern County had one travel-related dengue case last year, and none so far this year. Statewide, there were 200 travel-related cases reported last year, and 23 reported so far in 2026. Last year there were six locally transmitted cases confirmed in Los Angeles County and one in Imperial County, the CDPH reported. "I would say that it is a matter of when, and not if, there (will be) a locally transmitted case of dengue in Kern County," Dery said. "With the vector (Aedes mosquitoes) widely present, every travel case is a roll of the dice for local transmission and it will happen eventually." Travel-associated cases of dengue fever have been verified in other San Joaquin Valley counties, including Fresno, San Joaquin and Tulare counties, but so far, there are no verified cases of locally acquired dengue in the Central Valley. All local transmission cases in the state to date have been confined to Southern California. While about half the people who get the virus experience no symptoms, the illness can be quite painful and even fatal for some. Older adults, children, people with weakened immune systems and those with certain underlying health conditions are at greater risk of severe illness. Curtis Skidgel, manager of Westside Mosquito & Vector Control District in Taft, agrees that Kern will likely see local cases of the dengue virus. "I don't want to say anything that's going to scare the public, but it's very possible that a new disease, just like West Nile virus ... these things come in and out in waves." "If you've traveled somewhere that might have this disease and you're coming back and feeling sick, that's something that's really important," Skidgel said. "The mosquitoes don't come here infected. They bite somebody who's infected, or an animal that's infected, and then spread it to the population." It's important for travelers to know about these risks before they travel, so they can take preventative measures. And those who develop symptoms should talk to a healthcare provider and to make sure the provider knows about any recent travel. Infected persons should protect against further mosquito bites so that new mosquitoes don't transmit dengue to other people. The best way to protect yourself is to prevent mosquito bites altogether. Remove standing water around your home, use an EPA-registered insect repellent, wear long sleeves and pants outdoors, and limit outdoor activity during dawn and dusk when mosquitoes are most active. While the mosquito-to-human and human-to-mosquito cycle is the primary way dengue virus is spread, researchers in 2018 found evidence that female Aedes aegypti mosquitoes transmit the dengue virus to their offspring and infected male mosquitoes pass along the virus to females when they mate. Summer, he said, is beginning earlier in the spring and ending later in the fall, and that means biting mosquitoes are living longer and remaining active longer. "Warmer temperatures likely do impact activity later in the year, as mosquitoes will develop faster with warmer temperatures and will remain active for longer," said Kern Mosquito's Dery. The City Health Services Office (CHSO) provided the update during the Baguio City Council’s regular session on August 17, 2026. Representatives from the CHSO, Baguio General Hospital (BGH), and the Department of Health (DOH) were called to the session to discuss the city’s dengue situation and COVID-19 cases simultaneously. CHSO Head Celia Brillantes and City Epidemiology Surveillance Unit Head Donabel Panes said the city’s monitoring and data gathering in previous years have helped them identify the usual pattern of dengue cases, allowing them to anticipate the seasonal increase. From 2025 to 2026, the CHSO recorded a total of 1,657 dengue cases, including seven deaths. The cases included 833 males and 823 females, with 553 admitted patients. At the time of the discussion, nine patients were admitted and none had severe dengue. The CHSO clarified that the number of patients served by Baguio’s health facilities does not necessarily represent the number of dengue cases among Baguio residents. Of the more than 1,000 cases recorded in the two-year period, about 540 were Baguio residents, while the rest came from neighboring municipalities that also rely on the city’s health facilities. The CHSO also reported that dengue testing kits remain available at health centers, stressing that early detection remains important in preventing deaths, particularly because most dengue cases can be managed when patients seek medical attention early. Health officials explained that dengue cases tend to rise every three years. Weather conditions affect the mosquito population, with relative humidity, temperature, and rainfall influencing mosquito breeding. Intermittent rain can leave water in containers and other areas where mosquitoes breed, while continuous heavy rain may wash away these breeding sites. As another possible measure against dengue, the city is looking into the use of Wolbachia, a naturally occurring bacteria that can be introduced into Aedes aegypti mosquitoes, the main mosquitoes that transmit dengue. When mosquitoes carrying Wolbachia mate, the bacteria can reduce the ability of the mosquitoes to transmit dengue to people. According to the CHSO, Baguio is being considered by project proponents as a possible model for Wolbachia implementation that could eventually be expanded to other parts of the country. The city is still working on the necessary logistics and permits, and implementation will depend on approval from the DOH. A dengue vaccine is also not yet available for use in the country as it is still awaiting approval from the Food and Drug Administration (FDA). Health officials clarified that the vaccine under consideration is different from Dengvaxia. For now, the CHSO urges residents to continue following the DOH’s dengue prevention measures including the 4S strategy of searching for and destroying mosquito breeding places, securing self-protection, seeking early consultation, and supporting fogging or spraying in hotspot areas when warranted. The city is also still procuring dengue medicines for 2026. Medicines remain available, but health officials said they are hoping for faster procurement to ensure sufficient supplies. Meanwhile, DOH data showed 4,436 dengue cases across the Cordillera Administrative Region from January to August 8, 2026. content: Pasco County confirms case of dengue fever The Florida Department of Health in Pasco County issued a mosquito advisory Tuesday afternoon after confirming a human case of dengue fever. Pasco is now the fourth county in the Tampa Bay area to acquire the mosquito-borne illness in August, following Citrus, Hillsborough and Pinellas. Health officials issued an advisory reminding residents to take "drain and cover" precautions to reduce mosquito production and protect themselves. The advisory says DOH-Pasco and Pasco County Mosquito Control are coordinating surveillance and prevention efforts. What is dengue fever? Dengue fever is a viral disease spread to people through the bite of an infected Aedes aegypti mosquito. The most common symptom of the illness is a fever — hence its name — typically presenting like the flu, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Other common symptoms include aches and pains, nausea and vomiting, headaches, and a rash. The CDC says aches and pains typically occur behind the eyes and in the muscle joints and bones. DOH-Pasco says dengue can become severe within just a few hours. Officials urge you to keep an eye out for warning signs like blood in your nose, mouth, stool or vomit, belly pain and tenderness, restlessness, irritability and lethargy. For more information on the disease, visit the CDC website

content_title: Locally Acquired Dengue Fever Case Confirmed In Citrus County
content: CITRUS COUNTY, Fla. – Citrus County health officials have confirmed a case of locally acquired dengue fever, prompting local agencies to step up mosquito control and surveillance operations across the area. The Florida Department of Health in Citrus County (DOH-Citrus) announced the case and confirmed it is coordinating response efforts alongside Citrus County Mosquito Control. Planned measures include increased truck fogging, aerial larviciding, and targeted ground inspections to locate and treat mosquito breeding grounds. Dengue is not spread directly from person to person. Instead, the virus is transmitted through the bite of an infected Aedes aegypti mosquito, with symptoms typically showing up within 14 to 15 days of a bite. According to health officials, the infection usually presents as a flu-like illness marked by fever, severe muscle aches, joint pain, and occasionally a rash. Unlike many common viral infections, dengue generally does not cause respiratory symptoms. To lower the risk of infection, DOH-Citrus advises residents to take standard precautions against mosquito bites. These steps include wearing loose-fitting, long-sleeved shirts and long pants, as well as applying EPA-registered insect repellents to exposed skin and clothing. Health officials noted that EPA-registered repellents are safe and effective when used as directed, including for women who are pregnant or breastfeeding. Residents are also urged to eliminate standing water around their properties. Mosquitoes breed in standing water, so officials recommend draining birdbaths, flowerpots, buckets, garbage cans, pool covers, coolers, toys, and any other containers that collect rain or sprinkler runoff. Homeowners should also inspect and repair torn window, door, and patio screens to keep mosquitoes outside. The state health department maintains ongoing surveillance for multiple mosquito-borne illnesses across Florida, including dengue, malaria, chikungunya, West Nile virus, St. Louis encephalitis, and Eastern equine encephalitis. As part of statewide monitoring, residents are asked to report dead birds to the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission. Anyone experiencing symptoms consistent with dengue is advised to contact a healthcare provider. content_title: Dengue fever cases rise in Tampa Bay as health officials target disease-carrying mosquitoes
content: TAMPA, Fla. — Health officials across the Tampa Bay area are stepping up mosquito control efforts as the number of locally acquired dengue fever cases continues to rise. Hillsborough County says it recorded its first positive dengue fever test from an insect monitoring trap in July. Since then, 30 people have been confirmed to have contracted dengue fever from local mosquito bites, while another 21 preliminary tests are showing positive results. The county is targeting areas where health officials believe dengue-carrying mosquitoes are most active, using helicopters, trucks and crews equipped with backpack sprayers. On Monday night, three helicopters treated about 30,000 acres in an area east of the I-4 and I-275 corridor, where officials said they believe some of the first local cases were concentrated. The goal is to reduce populations of the Aedes aegypti mosquito, the species mostly responsible for transmitting dengue fever. But mosquito control officials say eliminating mosquitoes is only part of the effort. Gabriela Henderson with Hillsborough County Mosquito Services said Aedes aegypti mosquitoes are daytime biters, putting people who spend extended periods outdoors at risk. Health officials recommend wearing long pants and long sleeves and using mosquito repellent when spending time outside. Unlike illnesses such as the flu or COVID-19, dengue fever does not spread directly from person to person. “It is only spread through the bite of a mosquito,” Henderson said. A mosquito can become infected after biting a person who already has the virus and then transmit dengue when it bites another person. Hillsborough County Mosquito Services is also focusing on tire shops, which can provide ideal breeding conditions for Aedes aegypti mosquitoes. The mosquitoes can lay eggs in small amounts of standing water, making items such as discarded tires potential breeding sites. Officials are also asking residents to eliminate standing water around their homes. That includes checking sports equipment, garbage cans, children’s toys, tools and other outdoor items that can collect rainwater. Most people infected with dengue experience mild-to-moderate illness and recover on their own, health officials said. Symptoms can include fever, vomiting, body aches and skin rashes. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention estimates that about one in 20 people who become sick with dengue develop severe dengue, which can require hospitalization. Severe cases can cause internal bleeding, organ failure and other life-threatening complications. Reducing mosquito breeding grounds and taking precautions against mosquito bites can help limit the spread of dengue in the Tampa Bay area, health officials said

Across Haryana, 87 of the 147 cumulative cases have been reported by govt hospitals and 60 by private hospitals. According to the latest state vector-borne disease bulletin, Jhajjar has reported the highest number of cases at 28, followed by the city with 24. Together, the two districts account for 52 cases, or about 35% of the state’s total. The state has so far reported no confirmed dengue deaths this year. Five patients were still admitted to hospitals as of Aug 20, while 57 patients who had required hospitalisation had been discharged. Another 85 cases were treated on an outpatient basis. According to experts, warm and humid weather over the past few weeks was favourable for the breeding of Aedes mosquitoes, which transmit the dengue virus. Commonly seen symptoms of dengue include fever, headache, muscle and joint pain and a characteristic skin rash. Doctors emphasised the need for taking preventive measures to slow the spread of infections. They recommend wearing full-sleeved clothes, using mosquito repellents and cleaning any pools of stagnant water from containers, coolers, etc. Tired of too many ads?go ad free now Associate director of internal medicine at CK Birla Hospital (Gurgaon) Dr Tushar Tayal told TOI, “The overall number of patients presenting with dengue remains within the expected range and we have not observed an unusual increase in the severity of illness. Haryana reported 2,626 dengue cases in 2025, 6,469 in 2024 and 8,083 in 2023. This year, Karnal, with 13 cases, is the third worst-affected district. Hisar, Rewari and Sonipat have reported nine cases each, while Charkhi Dadri, Mahendragarh and Panchkula have recorded seven each. Faridabad has reported six cases so far, while Fatehabad and Panipat have recorded four each. Yamunanagar has reported four cases and Jind and Rohtak have three each. Kurukshetra has two cases, while Ambala has one. Bhiwani, Kaithal, Nuh and Palwal have not reported any cases so far.
